invitation: A moth, a grasshopper, a fox fur, a sunset. Take them in any order, not all at once, and notice what keeps catching your eye.

pieces.author: Virginia Woolf
pieces.note: A moth at a window on a September morning. Almost nothing happens, and the tension still builds. Watch how a tiny event is scaled up to the size of the world without the voice ever rising.
pieces.title: The Death of the Moth

pieces.author: Mary Oliver
pieces.note: Nineteen lines. Notice how long she stays on one small, physical description before she lets herself ask a big question. The last line is famous; read everything before it slowly.
pieces.title: The Summer Day

pieces.author: Katherine Mansfield
pieces.note: A woman goes to the park on a Sunday. Told almost entirely from inside her head, and the turn near the end is one of the cleanest gut-punches in the short story.
pieces.place: a public garden in France, published in London
pieces.title: Miss Brill

pieces.author: The Kinks (Ray Davies)
pieces.note: You'll know it. Listen as a lyricist this time: count the concrete nouns, and notice who the singer is and where he is standing.
pieces.title: Waterloo Sunset
